Gaming vs. Academic Performance

INFO 432 — Group 5 Final Report

Jeffrey Cheung, Drew Jones, Danny Eapen, Joel Thomas

August 11, 2026

1 Introduction

1.1 Research questions

Video games are the default leisure activity for a large share of college students, and the folk claim that gaming “ruins your grades” is repeated far more often than it is measured. This report takes a dataset of 8,000 students and asks three questions:

  1. Which lifestyle factors actually relate to grades? Gaming hours, study hours, sleep hours, class attendance, and a self-reported gaming addiction score are the five candidates. We test each one for a statistically significant relationship with grades.
  2. Where are the thresholds? A significant correlation says a relationship exists but not where it starts to matter. We look for the specific values — hours of gaming per day, hours of study — at which average performance visibly steps down.
  3. How well can grades be predicted? We build and compare regression models, and score them on students the model never saw, so the reported accuracy is honest.

1.2 The dataset

The data comes from the Kaggle dataset Gaming vs Academic Performance: 8,000 student records with 14 columns covering demographics, gaming habits, study habits, sleep, attendance, stress, and a final grade.

df_raw <- read_csv("data/Gaming_Academic_Performance.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

tibble(
  Column = names(df_raw),
  Type   = map_chr(df_raw, ~ class(.x)[1]),
  Example = map_chr(df_raw, ~ as.character(.x[1]))
) %>%
  tbl(caption = "Raw dataset structure (8,000 rows x 14 columns)")
Raw dataset structure (8,000 rows x 14 columns)

A caveat we state up front and return to in the limitations: this dataset is almost certainly simulated rather than collected. The relationships in it are far cleaner than real survey data ever is. Everything below is a correct application of the method to the data as given; none of it is a real-world claim about students.

Before deciding what to do with these 134 records, we checked whether they look like data entry errors or like genuine high performers:

bind_rows(
  over_100 %>%
    summarise(across(c(gaming_hours, study_hours, sleep_hours, attendance,
                       addiction_score), mean)) %>%
    mutate(Group = "Grades over 100", .before = 1),
  df_raw %>%
    filter(grades <= 100) %>%
    summarise(across(c(gaming_hours, study_hours, sleep_hours, attendance,
                       addiction_score), mean)) %>%
    mutate(Group = "Everyone else", .before = 1)
) %>%
  tbl(caption = "Profile of the over-100 records vs. the rest of the sample", digits = 2)
Profile of the over-100 records vs. the rest of the sample
Group gaming_hours study_hours sleep_hours attendance addiction_score
Grades over 100 2.66 8.65 7.37 84.32 7.20
Everyone else 4.11 5.41 6.48 79.81 9.95

They study more, game less, attend more, and score lower on addiction — exactly the profile of the strongest students. So these are informative cases, not noise. We capped them at 100 rather than dropping them, which keeps their predictor values in the sample at the cost of censoring their outcome. That censoring is carried forward as a known limitation in the modeling section.

df <- df_raw %>%
  mutate(grades = pmin(grades, 100)) %>%
  mutate(
    gender        = as.factor(gender),
    gaming_genre  = as.factor(gaming_genre),
    stress_level  = factor(stress_level, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
                           ordered = TRUE)
  )

write_csv(df, "data/cleaned_data.csv")

2.3 Post-cleaning distribution

p_hist <- ggplot(df, aes(x = grades)) +

ggsave("output/grade_distribution_graph.png", p_hist, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 110)
p_hist

The distribution is roughly normal with a visible spike at the top — that spike is the capping we just applied.

The gaming and addiction curves bend rather than run straight — the penalty per extra hour is not constant. That is the motivation for the squared terms in the modeling section.

4 Statistical testing

Source script: scripts/stat_testing.R

Setup. We use \(\alpha = 0.05\). For each factor the null hypothesis is that it has no relationship with grades; the alternative is that it does.

vars <- c("gaming_hours", "study_hours", "sleep_hours", "attendance",
          "addiction_score")

4.1 A note on method: why we dropped ANOVA

Our first version of this analysis used one-way ANOVA with factor(gaming_hours), factor(attendance), and so on. That was the wrong tool, and it gave us wrong answers. ANOVA compares a handful of groups, but these factors are continuous measurements, so factor() creates one group per distinct value:

cell_sizes <- tibble(
  variable     = vars,
  n_levels     = map_int(vars, ~ length(unique(df[[.x]]))),
  obs_per_cell = round(map_dbl(vars, ~ nrow(df) / length(unique(df[[.x]]))), 2)
)

tbl(cell_sizes, caption = "Distinct values per factor — why the ANOVA breaks down",
    digits = 2)
Distinct values per factor — why the ANOVA breaks down
variable n_levels obs_per_cell
gaming_hours 801 9.99
study_hours 901 8.88
sleep_hours 501 15.97
attendance 3472 2.30
addiction_score 2039 3.92

Attendance has 3,472 distinct values across 8,000 students — roughly two students per group. With cells that small there is almost nothing left to average within a group, which is exactly what the F test needs, and the test reported attendance as not significant when it actually is. The correlation tests and the regression below are the results we use; the ANOVA is kept in section 4.4 purely to document the comparison.

4.2 Test 1 — correlation of each factor with grades

This is the direct replacement for the one-way ANOVA. It asks the same question, “does this factor relate to grades”, but it uses the fact that the values are ordered instead of throwing that information away.

cor_results <- map_dfr(vars, function(v) {
  ct <- cor.test(df[[v]], df$grades)
  m  <- lm(df$grades ~ df[[v]])
  tibble(
    variable   = v,
    r          = round(unname(ct$estimate), 3),
    p_value    = ct$p.value,
    slope      = round(unname(coef(m)[2]), 3),
    r_squared  = round(summary(m)$r.squared, 4),
    conclusion = ifelse(ct$p.value < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject")
  )
})

write_csv(cor_results, "output/correlation_results.csv")

cor_results %>%
  mutate(p_value = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3, eps = 1e-300)) %>%
  tbl(caption = "Each factor tested against grades on its own")
Each factor tested against grades on its own
variable r p_value slope r_squared conclusion
gaming_hours -0.552 < 1e-300 -5.323 0.305 Reject H0
study_hours 0.733 < 1e-300 6.332 0.537 Reject H0
sleep_hours 0.249 1.10e-113 3.847 0.062 Reject H0
attendance 0.130 1.52e-31 0.250 0.017 Reject H0
addiction_score -0.496 < 1e-300 -2.192 0.246 Reject H0

Every factor, including attendance, is significant on its own. The slope column is the part worth quoting in a summary: it converts a p-value into plain language — one extra hour of study is worth about 6.3 grade points, one extra hour of gaming about -5.3.

4.3 Test 2 — all five factors in one regression

The correlations above look at one factor at a time, so a factor can look important just by riding along with another one. Putting them in the same model shows what each factor is worth once the others are already accounted for.

full_model <- lm(
  grades ~ gaming_hours + study_hours + sleep_hours + attendance + addiction_score,
  data = df
)

reg_results <- tidy(full_model) %>%
  mutate(conclusion = ifelse(p.value < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject"))

write_csv(reg_results, "output/regression_results.csv")

reg_results %>%
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 1e-300)) %>%
  tbl(caption = sprintf("Multiple regression, all five factors (adjusted R-squared = %.4f)",
                        summary(full_model)$adj.r.squared),
      digits = 4)
Multiple regression, all five factors (adjusted R-squared = 0.9106)
term estimate std.error statistic p.value conclusion
(Intercept) 7.0877 0.6616 10.7135 1.33e-26 Reject H0
gaming_hours -5.3381 0.0773 -69.0288 < 1e-300 Reject H0
study_hours 6.2532 0.0289 216.4639 < 1e-300 Reject H0
sleep_hours 3.7294 0.0516 72.2867 < 1e-300 Reject H0
attendance 0.2757 0.0064 42.9098 < 1e-300 Reject H0
addiction_score 0.0416 0.0355 1.1737 0.241 Fail to reject

Addiction score is the one factor that stops being significant here, and the reason is the 0.91 correlation with gaming hours we flagged in the EDA. It is not adding a separate effect; it is measuring gaming a second time. We report gaming hours as the real driver.

4.4 ANOVA vs. correlation, side by side

# The slow block: aov() is fitting thousands of levels per model.
anova_list <- list(
  gaming     = aov(df$grades ~ factor(df$gaming_hours)),
  study      = aov(df$grades ~ factor(df$study_hours)),
  sleep      = aov(df$grades ~ factor(df$sleep_hours)),
  attendance = aov(df$grades ~ factor(df$attendance)),
  addiction  = aov(df$grades ~ factor(df$addiction_score))
)

anova_tables <- map_dfr(names(anova_list), function(n) {
  tab <- as.data.frame(summary(anova_list[[n]])[[1]])
  tab$term  <- rownames(tab)
  tab$model <- n
  tab
})
write_csv(anova_tables, "output/anova_results.csv")

comparison <- tibble(
  variable     = vars,
  obs_per_cell = cell_sizes$obs_per_cell,
  anova_p      = map_dbl(anova_list, ~ summary(.x)[[1]][["Pr(>F)"]][1]),
  correct_p    = cor_results$p_value
) %>%
  mutate(
    anova_says   = ifelse(anova_p   < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject"),
    correct_says = ifelse(correct_p < 0.05, "Reject H0", "Fail to reject"),
    agrees       = ifelse(anova_says == correct_says, "", "DISAGREES")
  )

write_csv(comparison, "output/method_comparison.csv")

comparison %>%
  mutate(across(c(anova_p, correct_p), ~ format.pval(.x, digits = 3, eps = 1e-300))) %>%
  tbl(caption = "Where the wrong test changed the answer", digits = 2)
Where the wrong test changed the answer
variable obs_per_cell anova_p correct_p anova_says correct_says agrees
gaming_hours 9.99 < 1e-300 < 1e-300 Reject H0 Reject H0
study_hours 8.88 < 1e-300 < 1e-300 Reject H0 Reject H0
sleep_hours 15.97 5.65e-36 1.10e-113 Reject H0 Reject H0
attendance 2.30 0.114 1.52e-31 Fail to reject Reject H0 DISAGREES
addiction_score 3.92 5.26e-129 < 1e-300 Reject H0 Reject H0

4.5 Section conclusion

  • Study hours, gaming hours, sleep hours, and attendance are statistically significant predictors of grades, both individually and when tested together.
  • Addiction score is significant on its own but not once the other factors are included. It is a proxy for gaming hours, not a separate effect.
  • Attendance is significant — the opposite of what our original ANOVA concluded, and the reason we changed method.

5 Threshold analysis

Source script: scripts/threshold_analysis.R

Objective 2 is to find the values within each factor where performance shifts. We use two independent approaches so the cutoffs can be cross-checked: a decision tree, which picks its own split points, and binned averages, which show where the mean grade steps down.

5.1 Letter grades

Converting to a standard letter scale lets a threshold be stated in language a reader actually feels — “drops from A- to B+” rather than “drops 2.8 points”.

grade_breaks <- c(-Inf, 60, 63, 67, 70, 73, 77, 80, 83, 87, 90, 93, Inf)
grade_labels <- c("F", "D-", "D", "D+", "C-", "C", "C+", "B-", "B", "B+", "A-", "A")

to_letter <- function(x) cut(x, breaks = grade_breaks, labels = grade_labels,
                             right = FALSE)

df <- df %>% mutate(letter_grade = to_letter(grades))
write_csv(df, "data/cleaned_data_with_grades.csv")

df %>%
  count(letter_grade) %>%
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) %>%
  tbl(caption = "Letter grade distribution", digits = 1)
Letter grade distribution
letter_grade n pct
F 3131 39.1
D- 369 4.6
D 489 6.1
D+ 362 4.5
C- 348 4.3
C 468 5.8
C+ 382 4.8
B- 335 4.2
B 446 5.6
B+ 295 3.7
A- 268 3.4

5.2 Approach 1 — decision tree

reaction_time_ms is deliberately excluded. It is a consequence of gaming, not a cause of grades, so letting it split would steal credit from gaming_hours and make the cutoffs harder to interpret.

predictors <- c("gaming_hours", "study_hours", "sleep_hours", "attendance",
                "addiction_score", "device_usage", "social_activity", "age",
                "stress_level", "gaming_genre")

tree_data <- df %>%
  select(grades, all_of(predictors)) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

set.seed(432)
tree <- rpart(grades ~ ., data = tree_data, method = "anova",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0.005, maxdepth = 4, minbucket = 100))

png("output/decision_tree.png", width = 1600, height = 1000, res = 150)
rpart.plot(tree, type = 4, extra = 101, box.palette = "RdYlGn",
           main = "Where grades split: regression tree on student features")
invisible(dev.off())

rpart.plot(tree, type = 4, extra = 101, box.palette = "RdYlGn",
           main = "Where grades split: regression tree on student features")

# rpart stores splits per node in the order: primary, competitors, surrogates.
# Walk the frame to pick out only the primary split of each internal node.
frame    <- tree$frame
splits   <- as.data.frame(tree$splits)
internal <- which(frame$var != "<leaf>")

split_rows <- integer(0)
idx <- 1
for (i in internal) {
  split_rows <- c(split_rows, idx)
  idx <- idx + 1 + frame$ncompete[i] + frame$nsurrogate[i]
}

node_ids <- as.numeric(rownames(frame))[internal]

tree_splits <- tibble(
  depth       = floor(log2(node_ids)) + 1,
  # rpart makes rownames unique by appending .1, .2 ... strip that back off
  variable    = sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", rownames(splits)[split_rows]),
  split_value = round(splits$index[split_rows], 2),
  n_at_node   = frame$n[internal],
  mean_grade  = round(frame$yval[internal], 1)
) %>% arrange(depth, desc(n_at_node))

write_csv(tree_splits, "output/tree_splits.csv")
tbl(tree_splits, caption = "Tree split points — the candidate cutoffs", digits = 2)
Tree split points — the candidate cutoffs
depth variable split_value n_at_node mean_grade

2 gaming_hours 4.61 4236 52.4
2 gaming_hours 3.95 3764 81.4

3 study_hours 3.34 1929 39.5
3 study_hours 7.74 1832 90.4

4 gaming_hours 6.26 995 46.2

The tree splits on study hours first, then on gaming hours — and it picks a different gaming cutoff in each branch. That difference is itself a finding: the point at which gaming starts to cost depends on how much a student studies, which is the definition of an interaction, and it is why the modeling section tests one.

5.3 Approach 2 — binned averages

Mean grade per bin with a 95% confidence interval, so a visible step down can be checked against sampling noise before it gets called a threshold.

bin_specs <- list(
  gaming_hours    = seq(0, 8, by = 1),
  study_hours     = seq(1, 10, by = 1),
  sleep_hours     = seq(4, 9, by = 1),
  attendance      = seq(60, 100, by = 5),
  addiction_score = seq(-5, 25, by = 5)
)

binned_summary <- function(var, breaks) {
  df %>%
    mutate(bin = cut(.data[[var]], breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
    filter(!is.na(bin)) %>%
    group_by(bin) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), mean_grade = mean(grades),
              se = sd(grades) / sqrt(n()), .groups = "drop") %>%
    mutate(
      ci_low   = mean_grade - 1.96 * se,
      ci_high  = mean_grade + 1.96 * se,
      letter   = to_letter(mean_grade),
      variable = var,
      # Keep the within-variable ordering as a number. Stacking these tables would
      # otherwise merge the factor levels across variables and scramble which bin
      # follows which.
      bin_index = as.integer(bin),
      bin = as.character(bin)
    )
}

all_bins <- imap_dfr(bin_specs, ~ binned_summary(.y, .x))
write_csv(all_bins, "output/binned_means.csv")

for (v in names(bin_specs)) {
  d <- all_bins %>% filter(variable == v) %>%
    mutate(bin = fct_reorder(bin, bin_index))

  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = bin, y = mean_grade)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.85) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), width = 0.2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = letter), vjust = -0.8, size = 3.5) +
    labs(title = paste("Mean grade by", v),
         subtitle = "Error bars are 95% CIs; label is the letter grade of the bin mean",
         x = v, y = "Mean grade") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

  ggsave(paste0("output/binned_", v, ".png"), plot = p,
         width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 150)
  print(p)
}

5.4 The cutoffs

The steepest drop between neighbouring bins is the plain-language threshold for each factor.

threshold_summary <- all_bins %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  arrange(bin_index, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(drop = lag(mean_grade) - mean_grade,
         from_bin = lag(bin), from_letter = lag(letter)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(drop)) %>%
  slice_max(drop, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  transmute(
    variable,
    boundary   = paste(from_bin, "->", bin),
    grade_drop = round(drop, 1),
    shift      = paste(from_letter, "->", letter),
    n_after    = n,
    # A non-positive value means grades never actually step down for this factor,
    # so there is no threshold to report.
    threshold  = if_else(drop > 0, "yes", "none found")
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(grade_drop))

write_csv(threshold_summary, "output/threshold_summary.csv")
tbl(threshold_summary, caption = "Steepest grade drop per factor", digits = 1)
Steepest grade drop per factor
variable boundary grade_drop shift n_after threshold
addiction_score (5,10] -> (10,15] 13.4 C -> F 2575 yes
gaming_hours (1,2] -> (2,3] 7.9 B- -> C 970 yes
attendance (85,90] -> (90,95] -0.6 D+ -> D+ 1004 none found
sleep_hours (7,8] -> (8,9] -2.7 C- -> C 1580 none found
study_hours (8,9] -> (9,10] -3.8 B -> A- 861 none found

5.5 The whole distribution, not just the mean

p_mix <- df %>%
  mutate(bin = cut(gaming_hours, breaks = bin_specs$gaming_hours,
                   include.lowest = TRUE)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(bin)) %>%
  count(bin, letter_grade) %>%
  group_by(bin) %>%
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bin, y = prop, fill = letter_grade)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(direction = -1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Letter grade mix by daily gaming hours",
       x = "Gaming hours per day", y = "Share of students", fill = "Grade") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("output/letter_grade_by_gaming.png", p_mix, width = 9, height = 5, dpi = 150)
p_mix

A mean can move because everyone slipped a little or because a few students collapsed. This chart settles it: the entire distribution slides down as gaming hours rise, so the threshold is a shift in the whole population, not an artefact of a small tail.

6 Predictive modeling

Source script: scripts/modeling.R

Section 4 established which factors matter. This section asks the two questions a p-value cannot answer: what shape is each relationship, and how well does the model predict students it has never seen.

6.1 Train / test split

set.seed(432)
train_idx <- sample(nrow(df), size = floor(0.7 * nrow(df)))
train <- df[train_idx, ]
test  <- df[-train_idx, ]

cat(sprintf("Training on %d students, testing on %d\n", nrow(train), nrow(test)))
## Training on 5600 students, testing on 2400
# Grades were capped at 100 in cleaning, so a prediction above 100 cannot be right
# no matter what the formula says. Clamp before scoring.
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) sqrt(mean((actual - pmin(predicted, 100))^2))
r2   <- function(actual, predicted) {
  1 - sum((actual - pmin(predicted, 100))^2) / sum((actual - mean(actual))^2)
}

6.2 Candidate models

Each model adds something the previous one lacked, so the comparison shows whether the extra complexity earns its place.

models <- list(
  # Study hours alone, the strongest single predictor, as a floor to beat.
  study_only = grades ~ study_hours,

  # All five factors, straight line each. This is the model from section 4.3.
  main_effects = grades ~ gaming_hours + study_hours + sleep_hours + attendance +
                          addiction_score,

  # Gaming and addiction both bend rather than run straight (see the EDA scatterplots),
  # so add squared terms.
  with_curves = grades ~ gaming_hours + I(gaming_hours^2) + study_hours + sleep_hours +
                         attendance + addiction_score + I(addiction_score^2),

  # The tree split gaming at a different value in each branch, which is what an
  # interaction term represents: gaming costs more when study hours are low.
  with_interaction = grades ~ gaming_hours * study_hours + I(gaming_hours^2) +
                              sleep_hours + attendance + addiction_score +
                              I(addiction_score^2),

  # addiction_score correlates 0.91 with gaming_hours, so check what dropping it costs.
  no_addiction = grades ~ gaming_hours * study_hours + I(gaming_hours^2) +
                          sleep_hours + attendance
)

fits <- lapply(models, function(f) lm(f, data = train))

comparison_models <- imap_dfr(fits, function(m, name) {
  tibble(
    model      = name,
    n_terms    = length(coef(m)) - 1,
    train_rmse = round(rmse(train$grades, predict(m, train)), 3),
    test_rmse  = round(rmse(test$grades,  predict(m, test)),  3),
    test_r2    = round(r2(test$grades,    predict(m, test)),  4)
  )
})

write_csv(comparison_models, "output/model_comparison.csv")
tbl(comparison_models, caption = "Five candidate models, scored on the held-out test set",
    digits = 4)
Five candidate models, scored on the held-out test set
model n_terms train_rmse test_rmse test_r2
study_only 1 15.153 15.107 0.5352
main_effects 5 6.332 6.187 0.9220
with_curves 7 6.194 6.045 0.9256
with_interaction 8 5.936 5.850 0.9303
no_addiction 6 5.938 5.851 0.9303

train_rmse and test_rmse staying close is the sign we are not overfitting. If the test error were much worse than the training error, the model would be fitting noise.

6.3 Choosing the final model

Not simply the lowest test_rmse. Two of these land within 0.001 of each other, which is noise from this particular split rather than a real difference, and picking on raw minimum would hand us extra terms that do nothing. So we take the model with the fewest terms that gets within 1% of the best error.

best_rmse <- min(comparison_models$test_rmse)

best_name <- comparison_models %>%
  filter(test_rmse <= best_rmse * 1.01) %>%
  slice_min(n_terms, n = 1) %>%
  slice_min(test_rmse, n = 1) %>%
  pull(model)

cat(sprintf("Best test error: %.3f (%s)\n", best_rmse,
            comparison_models$model[which.min(comparison_models$test_rmse)]))
## Best test error: 5.850 (with_interaction)
cat(sprintf("Chosen for parsimony, within 1%% of best: %s\n", best_name))
## Chosen for parsimony, within 1% of best: no_addiction
# Refit the chosen structure on all 8,000 students for the coefficients we report.
final_model <- lm(models[[best_name]], data = df)

coefs <- tidy(final_model) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4)))

write_csv(coefs, "output/model_coefficients.csv")

coefs %>%
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 1e-300)) %>%
  tbl(caption = sprintf(
    "Final model coefficients, fit on all %d students (adjusted R-squared = %.4f, residual SE = %.2f grade points)",
    nrow(df), summary(final_model)$adj.r.squared, summary(final_model)$sigma),
    digits = 4)

6.4 Diagnostics

Students sitting exactly on the 100-point cap are flagged separately throughout. Their actual grade was truncated, so their residual is forced negative by the cap rather than by the model being wrong; mixing them into the trend line would misrepresent the fit.

diag_df <- tibble(
  fitted   = fitted(final_model),
  residual = resid(final_model),
  censored = df$grades >= 100
)

p1 <- ggplot(diag_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = censored), alpha = 0.25, size = 0.9) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "red") +
  # Loess on the uncensored students only, so the cap does not drag the line down.
  geom_smooth(data = filter(diag_df, !censored), method = "loess",
              colour = "blue", se = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "grey30", "TRUE" = "darkorange"),
                      labels = c("FALSE" = "normal", "TRUE" = "at 100 point cap"),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs fitted values",
       subtitle = paste("Blue line is flat across the normal range, so the model fits.",
                        "\nThe orange diagonal is the grade cap, not model error."),
       x = "Predicted grade", y = "Residual") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

ggsave("output/residuals_vs_fitted.png", p1, width = 8, height = 5.5, dpi = 150)
p1

p2 <- ggplot(filter(diag_df, !censored), aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq(alpha = 0.3) +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q plot of residuals",
       subtitle = "Excludes students at the 100 point cap. Points on the line means the normality assumption holds",
       x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("output/qq_residuals.png", p2, width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 150)
p2

test_pred <- tibble(
  actual    = test$grades,
  predicted = pmin(predict(final_model, test), 100)
)

p3 <- ggplot(test_pred, aes(x = actual, y = predicted)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "red") +
  labs(title = "Predicted vs actual grades, held-out test set",
       subtitle = "Red line is a perfect prediction",
       x = "Actual grade", y = "Predicted grade") +
  theme_minimal()

ggsave("output/predicted_vs_actual.png", p3, width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 150)
p3

7 Conclusions

7.1 What the analysis found

Summary of findings
Question Answer
Which factors relate to grades? Study hours, gaming hours, sleep hours and attendance are all significant (p < 0.05), individually and jointly.
Which factor matters most? Study hours — 6.33 grade points per additional hour, the largest single effect.
What about addiction score? Significant alone, but not once the others are controlled for. It correlates 0.91 with gaming hours, so it re-measures gaming rather than adding a separate effect.
Where are the thresholds? The tree and the binned means agree. Steepest drop overall: addiction_score at the (5,10] -> (10,15] boundary (13.4 grade points).
Is the relationship linear? No — gaming and addiction both bend, so squared terms improve the fit, and the gaming penalty is worse for students who study less (a real interaction).
How accurate is the model? Held-out test RMSE of 5.85 grade points, test R-squared 0.930. Train and test error are close, so the model is not overfitting.

7.2 Limitations

  1. Censored outcome. We capped grades at 100 in cleaning, so 573 students (7.2%) sit exactly on the ceiling. The model cannot distinguish a student who would have scored 101 from one who would have scored 118. A censored (tobit) regression handles this properly but is beyond the scope of this course project, so we flag it rather than paper over it.
  2. The data is almost certainly simulated. An adjusted R-squared near 0.93 is not something real survey data produces, and a 0.91 correlation between two supposedly independent variables is far too clean. Read these results as a demonstration of the method working on the data as given, not as a real-world finding about students.
  3. Observational, not causal. Students who game more also study less. The coefficients describe association. Nothing here proves that a student who cut their gaming would see their grade rise; that claim would need an experiment.
  4. Self-reported measures. Gaming hours, study hours, sleep, and the addiction score are the kind of variables that are systematically misreported in surveys, in predictable directions.

7.3 Reproducing this report

Everything above runs from the raw CSV. To regenerate the HTML and every file in output/:

rmarkdown::render("report/final_report.Rmd")

or, from a terminal at the project root:

Rscript scripts/render_report.R
